**Mark Roland Shand** (28 June 1951 – 23 April 2014) was an English travel writer and conservationist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3) He was the brother of Queen Camilla. Shand wrote four travel books, and as a BBC conservationist appeared in documentaries related to his journeys, most of which centred on the survival of elephants. His book _Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992. He was the chairman of Elephant Family, a wildlife foundation, which he co-founded in 2002.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-4)

## Family, education and marriage
[edit]
Mark Roland Shand was born on 28 June 1951, the third child and only son of Major Bruce Shand (1917–2006) and his wife, Rosalind Cubitt (1921–1994), daughter of the 3rd Baron Ashcombe and Sonia Rosemary Keppel, daughter of Alice Keppel. He was the brother of Queen Camilla (formerly Camilla Parker-Bowles) and Annabel Elliot.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)
Shand was educated first at [St Ronan's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Ronan's_School "St Ronan's School") in Kent[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-5) and then Milton Abbey School in Dorset. He was expelled from Milton Abbey for smoking cannabis,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-6) in response his father sent him to Australia to make a living on his own, where he had numerous jobs including working as a jackaroo on a station and a guard at an opal mine.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7) He later returned to London and worked as a porter at [Sotheby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's "Sotheby's"). Subsequently, he and his friend Harry Fane, the son of the 15th Earl of Westmorland, started a business of selling Cartier jewellery for a while.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8) He dated Caroline Kennedy, daughter of U.S. presidentJohn F. Kennedy and First LadyJacqueline Kennedy Onassis, in the mid-1970s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-9)

## Family, education and marriage
In 1990, Shand married Clio Goldsmith, a French former actress, daughter of Edward Goldsmith and niece of Sir James Goldsmith,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-10) who were all members of the prominent Goldsmith family. They lived in Rome and had a daughter, Ayesha (born 1st October 1994).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-11) Shand confirmed in 2010 that the couple were divorced.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-12) He was a godfather to one of the sons of Jemima Goldsmith, his former wife's cousin.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-13)
Shand published his first travel book _Skulduggery_ in 1987, based on an expedition to Irian Jaya in Indonesia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-14) He later became the author of _Travels on My Elephant_ (1992),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-15)_Queen of the Elephants_ (1996)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-16) and _River Dog: A Journey Down the Brahmaputra_ (2003).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-17)_Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-19)

## Family, education and marriage
He was featured in many documentaries for the BBC and the National Geographic Channel,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18) some related to his writings. Elephants were featured in many of his writings and other pursuits. An unabashed Indophile, the majority of his writings and TV features were Indo-Nostalgic. He also had a deep interest in Hinduism and Indian culture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)
As a BBC conservationist and travel writer, he wrote a book and the corresponding BBC documentary, _Queen of the Elephants_, based on the life of the first female mahout in recent times, Parbati Barua of Kaziranga. The book won the [Prix Litteraire d'Amis](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix%20litt%C3%A9raire%20de%20Trente%20millions%20d'amis "fr:Prix littéraire de Trente millions d'amis") award, providing publicity to the profession of mahouts, and to Kaziranga herself.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-21)

## Family, education and marriage
Shand was actively involved in the conservation of the Asian elephant and co-founded a charity called Elephant Family in 2002.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-22) His book _Travels on My Elephant_ was about his adventure with "Tara" (his elephant) in India, who was the inspiration for the charity.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-23) Shand was also a patron of Anti-Slavery International,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-24) a member of the Royal Geographical Society and an honorary Chief Wildlife Warden of Assam.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18)
In 2014, Mark Shand received "the Conservationist of the Year 2014" award, and the Fragile Rhino award of The Perfect World Foundation at the Conservation Gala Dinner "Save The Rhino" in Gothenburg, Sweden. Shand had been expected to attend as a guest of honour, but died unexpectedly before the event.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-25)

Elephant Family lives on, however, with the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall as its new royal presidents, and with Prince William taking up the cause as well. In November, the actor Owen Wilson and Lexi Bowes-Lyon will host an Elephants Forever auction at Sotheby’s in New York. And Ruth Powys is organizing a celebrity rickshaw race in India, with 43 rickshaws, decorated by famous artists, traversing more than 300 miles across Madhya Pradesh state to Kipling Camp, where Mark’s beloved Tara (the star of his 1991 best-seller, _Travels on My Elephant_) enjoys her retirement.
People routinely compared Mark Shand to Tarzan, Indiana Jones, and Sir Richard Burton (who discovered the source of the Nile, penetrated Mecca in disguise, and translated the Kama Sutra into English). The late Nigel Dempster, London’s top society columnist for decades, dubbed him “He-Man Shand.”
“There’s no doubt about it, Shand was the Tarzan figure in reality,” says Don McCullin, the British war photographer who traveled with Shand to the region of New Guinea where Michael Rockefeller had disappeared, presumably a victim of cannibals. McCullin, a generation older and a mentor to Shand, adds, “Women fell like autumn leaves into his arms.”
Among those reputedly linked to Shand before his 1990 marriage to Clio Goldsmith (a niece of the Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith): Lee Radziwill _and_ her niece Caroline Kennedy; Caroline Windisch-Graetz Cushing Graham; Liz Dent-Brocklehurst, _before_ she married Shand’s rich uncle Lord Ashcombe; Bianca Jagger, _after_ she divorced Mick; and Marie Helvin, as she was divorcing David Bailey. At the time of his death, he was rumored to be involved with the bosomy London socialite Nancy Dell’Olio. (He denied it; she didn’t.)

“I thought of him as Crocodile Dundee,” says Julia Roberts, who made two PBS documentaries with Shand in the late 1990s, _Orangutans,_ filmed in Borneo, and _Wild Horses of Mongolia._ “But he wasn’t a chauvinist and he wasn’t a show-off.” For Goldie Hawn, who co-starred with Shand in _The Elephants of India_ for PBS, in 1996, he was “a real Renaissance guy” _and_ “sort of a rogue—irrepressible, contagious, maddening.”
“My uncle had this charmed existence,” says Camilla’s son, the journalist Tom Parker Bowles. “Mark was either crossing India on a private jet or on an elephant. He wasn’t very good at Economy.”
Mark Roland Shand was born on June 28, 1951, to Major Bruce Shand and the Honorable Rosalind Maud Cubitt. His father’s family had made its money importing calico fabric from India. Major Shand, a Sandhurst graduate, served as an officer in the 12th Royal Lancers during World War II. He spent two years in a German prisoner-of-war camp and was twice awarded the Military Cross for bravery. “Mark’s father was one of the guys on whom _The Great Escape_ was based,” says writer Gita Mehta, referring to the 1963 movie starring Steve McQueen. Don McCullin recalls, “Major Shand was the archetypal English gentleman with decorations, good manners, impeccable dress. That was quite a hallmark for Mark to live up to.” Mark’s mother was the daughter of Roland Cubitt, the third Lord Ashcombe, whose great-grandfather had made a fortune building much of Belgravia and Pimlico in the first half of the 19th century. _Her_ mother, Sonia Keppel, was a daughter of Alice Keppel—the official mistress of King Edward VII.

Bruce Shand and Rosalind Cubitt made a highly attractive couple when they married, in 1946, at St. Paul’s, Knightsbridge, with a reception following at Claridge’s. Camilla was born the following year, and Annabel two years after that. They lived in the village of Plumpton, about 50 miles south of London. Their house, the Laines, was surrounded by Rosalind’s garden, which had been laid out by the distinguished landscape designer Russell Page. Bruce Shand spent weeknights at the family’s residence in London, where he was a partner in the Mayfair wine merchants Block, Grey and Block. His passions were polo and fox-hunting, and from 1956 to 1975 he was Master of Southdown Foxhounds.
“We had this enchanted childhood,” says Annabel Elliot. “Unlike a lot of our generation, we had this incredibly warm, easy relationship with our parents. We didn’t have nannies. All our friends growing up would immediately be drawn to my mother. She was completely straightforward, and one of the warmest, kindest people.”
“Life at the Laines was wonderful,” agrees interior decorator Jane Churchill, whose parents were best friends with the Shands. “The odd thing for that sort of family is they were brought up in a completely unsnobbish way. That’s where Camilla has the edge. It’s no different to her to talk to a duke or a dustman. And Mark was the same.” Another old family friend, antique dealer Duncan McLaren, remembers, “Mark was always the joker in the pack, the one who was getting up to trouble. His mother _adored_ him. His sisters _adored_ him.”
Annabel told me that a few years before their mother died, in 1994, “Camilla and I were having lunch with her. And she said, ‘Darlings, I’ve always been completely fair between the three of you, haven’t I?’ Camilla’s and my jaws dropped. Because that was _not_ the way it was. Literally, Mark could do no wrong. There’s the theme that should run through your whole story: Mark, having been worshipped by my mother, was spoiled by women his whole life.”

Annabel recounted the unsuccessful effort to get her brother into Eton: “By the time he’d had about 10 math tutors, it was clear there was no hope. So he went to this ropy school called Milton Abbey.” At 16, Mark was expelled for smoking marijuana. His father decided it was time for him to shape up. Along with William Waldorf Astor III, Mark was sent to work on a sheep farm in Australia for six months. “We were each given about £100 and a plane ticket,” says William Astor.
As luck would have it, on their stopover in Delhi, the 17-year-olds ran into the grandson of Lord Mountbatten, the last viceroy of India, and spent the next several weeks touring the subcontinent in deluxe style, going from lunch at the Indian presidential palace to the Taj Mahal under army protection. In Jaipur, the boys were received by the Maharani Ayesha and her son, Prince Jagat, both of whom would become Shand’s close friends. After putting in their time in the Australian outback, “riding horses and getting thousands of sheep ready to be sheared,” Astor recalls, they spent four months meandering through Nepal, Afghanistan, and Turkey in a jeep.
Lee Radziwill got to know Mark Shand in the late 1960s at Helmsley, the shooting estate in Yorkshire that her husband Prince Stanislas Radziwill leased with Harry Ashcombe, the younger brother of Mark’s mother. “I was always so happy when I knew Mark was coming,” she says. “It was so dreary when he didn’t.”
For a long time Shand assumed that he would inherit a substantial fortune from his thrice-married yet childless Uncle Harry (known as Mad Harry). The fourth Baron Ashcombe was chairman of Holland, Hannen & Cubitts, which controlled the family’s vast property holdings in London. Unfortunately, as William Astor puts it, “he was the nicest man—and the worst businessman. He owned Pimlico and he sold it for nothing.” (According to _The Telegraph,_ the Pimlico estate, covering 27 acres, including 480 houses, was sold for £4.4 million in 1970.)

By then they were spending every February with Prince Jagat at his ancient fort in the center of Jaipur, hunting for gems by day and carousing by night. July and August were reserved for Bali, where they built, in Shand’s description, “a beautiful Robinson Crusoe house on a surfers’ beach. We lived a bohemian life, chilled-out and very anti-social.” Fane recalled, “We did some amazing trips. We did this huge sail through Indonesia in a dug-out tree.” But, Fane added, “Mark came to me one day and said, ‘Look, I really want to give up work. I want to spend my life out here, not back in the other world. Let’s sell everything and buy a boat.’ ”
Fane returned to work at the end of the summer while Shand spent the next nine months restoring a 28-foot yacht in Fiji. “Mark sold his flat in London,” Fane said. “He sold every single thing he had for this boat.” In March 1982, Mark, along with a more experienced local sailor, set out from Fiji, to Honiara, in the Solomon Islands, dropping anchor in the harbor just in time for a hurricane to hit. “The boat was like a bucking bronco,” Shand wrote. “I decided we had to get off, otherwise we were dead…. We both were cut to pieces, lacerated by the coral while being swept ashore…. The boat had no chance…. I saw her rise up once more, topple backwards, and snap in two like a matchstick. I was numb. My dream had ended. I had lost everything.”
Shand and Clio Goldsmith, at home in London, 1998; they were married from 1990 to 2009.
By Derry Moore/Camera Press/Redux.

Shortly after he returned to London, Shand was introduced to war photographer Don McCullin, who asked Mark to accompany him on an expedition to the Mentawai Islands, in Indonesia, to photograph the lost Sakkudei people. After 18 years covering wars from Vietnam to El Salvador for the London _Sunday Times,_ McCullin had been pushed out by the new Murdoch regime, and, as he wrote in his 1992 autobiography, _Unreasonable Behaviour,_ he wanted to “get rid of the rubbish in my mind and record the disappearing tribes of the world, before it’s too late.” McCullin, the son of a fishmonger, told me, “When I first met Mark, I didn’t think he’d be my cup of tea. He was brought up in that kind of aristocratic world. But he chose a freer world.”
In 1985, Shand and McCullin, joined by Fane, made their expedition to New Guinea (then called Irian Jaya). “One day, we found ourselves in this strange place called Otsjanep, which has a reputation for cannibalism,” recalls the photographer. “We were chased by what I thought were pirates, but they were Indonesian paramilitaries, and they surrounded us. They were pointing M16s at us. This guy who was looking after us was somebody Mark had found in Jakarta’s bus station—he did all the interpretation. The paramilitaries said, ‘You’ve been looking for skulls,’ and we said, ‘No we haven’t.’ But Mark and Harry _had_ bought some human skulls and had them in biscuit tins on the boat. The guy that Mark picked up at the bus station started saying about Harry, ‘This man friend of the Queen.’ And then he pointed to Mark: ‘This man friend of prime minister of England.’ In fact, Mark’s uncle was Sir Geoffrey Howe, the foreign secretary. He had nothing to say about me. I had no pedigree at all. But he saved our asses.”

Around that time, Mark began a romance with Marie Helvin, the sultry British _Vogue_ cover girl whose marriage to photographer David Bailey was near an end. In her 2007 book, _The Autobiography,_ Helvin described their first encounter, at a London dinner party: “I still remember … the sheer heat I felt when he said hello…. It didn’t take long for that initial ember of attraction to explode into a bonfire of lust.” Nonetheless, she says she turned him down when he proposed marriage, in late 1987.
That June, however, Mark had met his future wife, Clio Goldsmith, at a ball given by her uncle Jimmy Goldsmith at Cliveden, the former Astor stately home in Buckinghamshire. Clio, a daughter of Jimmy’s older brother, Teddy Goldsmith, had been previously married to Pirelli-tire heir Carlo Puri Negri. “For dinner it was a very serious older crowd, all these English politicians and aristocrats,” says Clio. “Exactly at midnight, these double doors opened and in stepped Mark and Imran Khan with a whole bunch of young, groovy people behind them. Mark and I looked at each other and that was it. We sat and we talked till six o’clock in the morning.”
Mark and Clio seemed custom-made for each other. Her father was an ecologist, polemicist, and philosopher, who traveled extensively among the tribal peoples of Africa and Asia. Clio recalled he would dictate to his secretary in full Masai gear from Kenya. Her mother was an English beauty aptly named Jill Pretty. As a young girl, Clio devoured the exotic adventure novels of the 19th-century English writer H. Rider Haggard, and Sir Richard Burton was her idol. She left home when she was 16, modeled in Paris for a few years, then in 1980 made her first film, in Rome. “It was called _La Cicala,_ the Gypsy girl,” she said. “That was me. I always played Gypsy girls or prostitutes.” When she met Mark, she had been “living in a car in Guatemala, being a textile dealer.”

“A few months after I met Mark, he got up one morning and he said to me, ‘I’ve got this fabulous idea. I’m going to travel India on an elephant.’ I said, ‘Wow, can I come too?’ ‘No, you can’t, because it’s a man’s expedition.’ ”
Shand published his first book, _Skulduggery,_ about his New Guinea trip, in 1987. Four years later he produced the unexpectedly affecting _Travels on My Elephant,_ which recounts his 600-mile journey on a she-elephant named Tara from the Bay of Bengal to the world’s oldest elephant market, on the Ganges River. It became an enormous best-seller and won him the British Travel Writer of the Year Award. Shand’s third book, _Queen of the Elephants,_ about the first female mahout (elephant driver), Parbati Barua, won the 1996 Thomas Cook Travel Book Award in Britain and the Prix Littéraire 30 Millions d’Amis in France, and was accompanied by a BBC documentary. Clio recalls, “We went off together on that one…. Mark and I had eight years of complete bliss. After that it got complicated.”
They had married three years after they met, in 1990, at the Laines. Clio wore a cream lace dress by Ossie Clark, and the wedding cake was in the shape of the Taj Mahal. They took a four-month honeymoon, Clio says. “Marie-Hélène de Rothschild lent us her house in Marrakech. Then we went down the Nile and to Singapore and Bali, to Mark’s house, where my father joined us.”

Ayesha Shand was born in 1994. As far as Mark was concerned she was named after Ayesha of Jaipur, but, for Clio, the name came from Haggard’s 1887 novel, _She: A History of Adventure,_ in which Ayesha is the 2,000-year-old white queen ruling over a tribe of central-African savages. “We bought a house at the bottom of a valley in Wiltshire,” Clio told me. “Very dark, very miserable, very isolated. Mark set off traveling, and I was alone with this baby. I had had a terrible birth, so I had to be operated on. And I was very traumatized.”
The success of his books had given Shand the legitimacy, the sense of purpose, that he’d always lacked. “He was looking for something,” says William Astor. “And it wasn’t until he met an elephant that he found it, and redeemed himself.” The books and the TV documentaries with Goldie Hawn and Julia Roberts that followed also made Shand a celebrity, complete with groupies. Astor says that the in-joke around London was that “for a whole generation of English upper-class girls, their gap year was going to India, going to the elephant camp, meeting Mark, sleeping with Mark. It was like a rite of passage.”
“One day I decided I’ve got to react,” Clio recalled. “He’d been months away, so I wrote him a note that said, ‘Gone to live in Rome with Ayesha. If you want to join us, here’s the plane ticket.’ ” For the next seven years, Mark made a halfhearted attempt to cohabit with his wife and daughter in Italy. “He was so terrible! He wouldn’t utter a word of Italian. But I loved him. In a big, big way. We decided we should go back to England and make a fresh start. Unfortunately, by that time I’d lost him, basically. And I couldn’t live with Mark in that indifferent way. It was too painful. He got very very obsessed by his charity, Elephant Family. Which was fantastic for him, and I truly recognized how wonderful it was. But our marriage just broke to pieces.” Shand and Goldsmith divorced in 2009.

Shand had launched Elephant Family in 2002, with Ayesha of Jaipur and London banker Sir Evelyn de Rothschild as its leading patrons. In the afterword of the 2012 edition of _Travels on My Elephant,_ Shand explained the organization’s mission:
Ninety percent of the Asian elephant population had been wiped out in the previous hundred years. Ninety-five percent of their forest homes had been destroyed to make way for plantations, farms, mines, roads, railways and villages…. The last remaining elephants were forced into tiny pockets of forest where they were competing with their human neighbours for food, water and space…. In India alone, a person kills an elephant and an elephant kills a person every single day of the year…. Elephant Family is dedicated to ending this daily battle.
Elephant Family didn’t really get going until 2004, when Shand found the 26-year-old Ruth Powys, daughter of an evangelical preacher from the north of England, who would turn out to be his perfect creative, administrative, and romantic partner. “They became this incredible force together,” says Ruth’s twin sister, Mary Powys, who joined the charity in 2008. “They were on and off for many years, but what was consistent was the huge respect and love between them. Because together they were making stuff happen.” When I asked Ruth about her relationship with Shand, she said, “Basically, I comforted him through his horrible divorce.”
The first big fund-raiser Shand and Powys pulled together was the 2006 Elephant Durbar at the Petersham Nurseries, outside London, which was attended by Prince Charles and Camilla, who had wed the previous year. Then came the Elephant Parade in London in 2010, Jungle City in Edinburgh in 2011, and the first Fabergé Big Egg Hunt, in London in 2012. Henry Wyndham, a chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, estimates the Sotheby’s auctions that were part of these events took in as much as $10 million.

In July 2013, the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall hosted Elephant Family’s Animal Ball, with drinks at Clarence House followed by dinner next door at Lancaster House. That November, Mark met up with his sister and brother-in-law on their official tour of India, taking them to see some of Elephant Family’s projects. “My stepfather adored him,” says Tom Parker Bowles. “They were very similar in their views. They just got on. And when they went to India, Mummy said, ‘Thank God for Mark. I’ve never been happier to see my little brother in my whole life.’ ”
“Mark was absolutely full of his new role being sort of the palace wit,” his art historian friend John Richardson says. “And Charles finally had a buddy. Mark put everybody at their ease. And he had all these stories to tell. And he told them brilliantly.”
Mark could also be relentless and rude. He wanted _more_ artists, _more_ press, _more_ real-estate tycoons to place his eggs around their buildings and sponsor them for $10,000 each. “His view was ‘You’re so fucking rich, give me the fucking money,’ ” says Ben Elliot, whose international concierge company, Quintessentially, helped organize the project. “But to get shit done, you have to be relentless.” Even the devoted Annabel admits, “He was a user and abuser; we all knew that in the family. But we all went back for more. And that’s the interesting thing.”
“When Mark died, his diary was full,” notes Mary Powys. “There were at least eight cities that had expressed interest in hosting Big Egg Hunts, including Hong Kong.” Shand’s Indian friend Uma Dubash, the sister of the last Maharaja of Morvi, told me, “There’s still a lot of work to be done for the Asian elephant, but the ground has been broken by Mark. He became the Elephant Man for a lot of Indians.”

**Mark Roland Shand** (28 June 1951 – 23 April 2014) was an English travel writer and conservationist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3) He was the brother of Queen Camilla. Shand wrote four travel books, and as a BBC conservationist appeared in documentaries related to his journeys, most of which centred on the survival of elephants. His book _Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992. He was the chairman of Elephant Family, a wildlife foundation, which he co-founded in 2002.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-4)

## Family, education and marriage
[edit]
Mark Roland Shand was born on 28 June 1951, the third child and only son of Major Bruce Shand (1917–2006) and his wife, Rosalind Cubitt (1921–1994), daughter of the 3rd Baron Ashcombe and Sonia Rosemary Keppel, daughter of Alice Keppel. He was the brother of Queen Camilla (formerly Camilla Parker-Bowles) and Annabel Elliot.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)
Shand was educated first at [St Ronan's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Ronan's_School "St Ronan's School") in Kent[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-5) and then Milton Abbey School in Dorset. He was expelled from Milton Abbey for smoking cannabis,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-6) in response his father sent him to Australia to make a living on his own, where he had numerous jobs including working as a jackaroo on a station and a guard at an opal mine.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7) He later returned to London and worked as a porter at [Sotheby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's "Sotheby's"). Subsequently, he and his friend Harry Fane, the son of the 15th Earl of Westmorland, started a business of selling Cartier jewellery for a while.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8) He dated Caroline Kennedy, daughter of U.S. presidentJohn F. Kennedy and First LadyJacqueline Kennedy Onassis, in the mid-1970s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-9)

## Family, education and marriage
In 1990, Shand married Clio Goldsmith, a French former actress, daughter of Edward Goldsmith and niece of Sir James Goldsmith,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-10) who were all members of the prominent Goldsmith family. They lived in Rome and had a daughter, Ayesha (born 1st October 1994).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-11) Shand confirmed in 2010 that the couple were divorced.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-12) He was a godfather to one of the sons of Jemima Goldsmith, his former wife's cousin.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-13)
Shand published his first travel book _Skulduggery_ in 1987, based on an expedition to Irian Jaya in Indonesia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-14) He later became the author of _Travels on My Elephant_ (1992),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-15)_Queen of the Elephants_ (1996)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-16) and _River Dog: A Journey Down the Brahmaputra_ (2003).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-17)_Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-19)

## Family, education and marriage
He was featured in many documentaries for the BBC and the National Geographic Channel,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18) some related to his writings. Elephants were featured in many of his writings and other pursuits. An unabashed Indophile, the majority of his writings and TV features were Indo-Nostalgic. He also had a deep interest in Hinduism and Indian culture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)
As a BBC conservationist and travel writer, he wrote a book and the corresponding BBC documentary, _Queen of the Elephants_, based on the life of the first female mahout in recent times, Parbati Barua of Kaziranga. The book won the [Prix Litteraire d'Amis](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix%20litt%C3%A9raire%20de%20Trente%20millions%20d'amis "fr:Prix littéraire de Trente millions d'amis") award, providing publicity to the profession of mahouts, and to Kaziranga herself.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-21)
texts.4:
## Family, education and marriage
Shand was actively involved in the conservation of the Asian elephant and co-founded a charity called Elephant Family in 2002.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-22) His book _Travels on My Elephant_ was about his adventure with "Tara" (his elephant) in India, who was the inspiration for the charity.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-23) Shand was also a patron of Anti-Slavery International,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-24) a member of the Royal Geographical Society and an honorary Chief Wildlife Warden of Assam.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18)
In 2014, Mark Shand received "the Conservationist of the Year 2014" award, and the Fragile Rhino award of The Perfect World Foundation at the Conservation Gala Dinner "Save The Rhino" in Gothenburg, Sweden. Shand had been expected to attend as a guest of honour, but died unexpectedly before the event.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-25)

texts.3:
Elephant Family lives on, however, with the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall as its new royal presidents, and with Prince William taking up the cause as well. In November, the actor Owen Wilson and Lexi Bowes-Lyon will host an Elephants Forever auction at Sotheby’s in New York. And Ruth Powys is organizing a celebrity rickshaw race in India, with 43 rickshaws, decorated by famous artists, traversing more than 300 miles across Madhya Pradesh state to Kipling Camp, where Mark’s beloved Tara (the star of his 1991 best-seller, _Travels on My Elephant_) enjoys her retirement.
People routinely compared Mark Shand to Tarzan, Indiana Jones, and Sir Richard Burton (who discovered the source of the Nile, penetrated Mecca in disguise, and translated the Kama Sutra into English). The late Nigel Dempster, London’s top society columnist for decades, dubbed him “He-Man Shand.”
“There’s no doubt about it, Shand was the Tarzan figure in reality,” says Don McCullin, the British war photographer who traveled with Shand to the region of New Guinea where Michael Rockefeller had disappeared, presumably a victim of cannibals. McCullin, a generation older and a mentor to Shand, adds, “Women fell like autumn leaves into his arms.”
Among those reputedly linked to Shand before his 1990 marriage to Clio Goldsmith (a niece of the Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith): Lee Radziwill _and_ her niece Caroline Kennedy; Caroline Windisch-Graetz Cushing Graham; Liz Dent-Brocklehurst, _before_ she married Shand’s rich uncle Lord Ashcombe; Bianca Jagger, _after_ she divorced Mick; and Marie Helvin, as she was divorcing David Bailey. At the time of his death, he was rumored to be involved with the bosomy London socialite Nancy Dell’Olio. (He denied it; she didn’t.)
texts.4:
“I thought of him as Crocodile Dundee,” says Julia Roberts, who made two PBS documentaries with Shand in the late 1990s, _Orangutans,_ filmed in Borneo, and _Wild Horses of Mongolia._ “But he wasn’t a chauvinist and he wasn’t a show-off.” For Goldie Hawn, who co-starred with Shand in _The Elephants of India_ for PBS, in 1996, he was “a real Renaissance guy” _and_ “sort of a rogue—irrepressible, contagious, maddening.”
“My uncle had this charmed existence,” says Camilla’s son, the journalist Tom Parker Bowles. “Mark was either crossing India on a private jet or on an elephant. He wasn’t very good at Economy.”
Mark Roland Shand was born on June 28, 1951, to Major Bruce Shand and the Honorable Rosalind Maud Cubitt. His father’s family had made its money importing calico fabric from India. Major Shand, a Sandhurst graduate, served as an officer in the 12th Royal Lancers during World War II. He spent two years in a German prisoner-of-war camp and was twice awarded the Military Cross for bravery. “Mark’s father was one of the guys on whom _The Great Escape_ was based,” says writer Gita Mehta, referring to the 1963 movie starring Steve McQueen. Don McCullin recalls, “Major Shand was the archetypal English gentleman with decorations, good manners, impeccable dress. That was quite a hallmark for Mark to live up to.” Mark’s mother was the daughter of Roland Cubitt, the third Lord Ashcombe, whose great-grandfather had made a fortune building much of Belgravia and Pimlico in the first half of the 19th century. _Her_ mother, Sonia Keppel, was a daughter of Alice Keppel—the official mistress of King Edward VII.
texts.5:
Bruce Shand and Rosalind Cubitt made a highly attractive couple when they married, in 1946, at St. Paul’s, Knightsbridge, with a reception following at Claridge’s. Camilla was born the following year, and Annabel two years after that. They lived in the village of Plumpton, about 50 miles south of London. Their house, the Laines, was surrounded by Rosalind’s garden, which had been laid out by the distinguished landscape designer Russell Page. Bruce Shand spent weeknights at the family’s residence in London, where he was a partner in the Mayfair wine merchants Block, Grey and Block. His passions were polo and fox-hunting, and from 1956 to 1975 he was Master of Southdown Foxhounds.
“We had this enchanted childhood,” says Annabel Elliot. “Unlike a lot of our generation, we had this incredibly warm, easy relationship with our parents. We didn’t have nannies. All our friends growing up would immediately be drawn to my mother. She was completely straightforward, and one of the warmest, kindest people.”
“Life at the Laines was wonderful,” agrees interior decorator Jane Churchill, whose parents were best friends with the Shands. “The odd thing for that sort of family is they were brought up in a completely unsnobbish way. That’s where Camilla has the edge. It’s no different to her to talk to a duke or a dustman. And Mark was the same.” Another old family friend, antique dealer Duncan McLaren, remembers, “Mark was always the joker in the pack, the one who was getting up to trouble. His mother _adored_ him. His sisters _adored_ him.”
Annabel told me that a few years before their mother died, in 1994, “Camilla and I were having lunch with her. And she said, ‘Darlings, I’ve always been completely fair between the three of you, haven’t I?’ Camilla’s and my jaws dropped. Because that was _not_ the way it was. Literally, Mark could do no wrong. There’s the theme that should run through your whole story: Mark, having been worshipped by my mother, was spoiled by women his whole life.”
texts.6:
Annabel recounted the unsuccessful effort to get her brother into Eton: “By the time he’d had about 10 math tutors, it was clear there was no hope. So he went to this ropy school called Milton Abbey.” At 16, Mark was expelled for smoking marijuana. His father decided it was time for him to shape up. Along with William Waldorf Astor III, Mark was sent to work on a sheep farm in Australia for six months. “We were each given about £100 and a plane ticket,” says William Astor.
As luck would have it, on their stopover in Delhi, the 17-year-olds ran into the grandson of Lord Mountbatten, the last viceroy of India, and spent the next several weeks touring the subcontinent in deluxe style, going from lunch at the Indian presidential palace to the Taj Mahal under army protection. In Jaipur, the boys were received by the Maharani Ayesha and her son, Prince Jagat, both of whom would become Shand’s close friends. After putting in their time in the Australian outback, “riding horses and getting thousands of sheep ready to be sheared,” Astor recalls, they spent four months meandering through Nepal, Afghanistan, and Turkey in a jeep.
Lee Radziwill got to know Mark Shand in the late 1960s at Helmsley, the shooting estate in Yorkshire that her husband Prince Stanislas Radziwill leased with Harry Ashcombe, the younger brother of Mark’s mother. “I was always so happy when I knew Mark was coming,” she says. “It was so dreary when he didn’t.”
For a long time Shand assumed that he would inherit a substantial fortune from his thrice-married yet childless Uncle Harry (known as Mad Harry). The fourth Baron Ashcombe was chairman of Holland, Hannen & Cubitts, which controlled the family’s vast property holdings in London. Unfortunately, as William Astor puts it, “he was the nicest man—and the worst businessman. He owned Pimlico and he sold it for nothing.” (According to _The Telegraph,_ the Pimlico estate, covering 27 acres, including 480 houses, was sold for £4.4 million in 1970.)
texts.9:
By then they were spending every February with Prince Jagat at his ancient fort in the center of Jaipur, hunting for gems by day and carousing by night. July and August were reserved for Bali, where they built, in Shand’s description, “a beautiful Robinson Crusoe house on a surfers’ beach. We lived a bohemian life, chilled-out and very anti-social.” Fane recalled, “We did some amazing trips. We did this huge sail through Indonesia in a dug-out tree.” But, Fane added, “Mark came to me one day and said, ‘Look, I really want to give up work. I want to spend my life out here, not back in the other world. Let’s sell everything and buy a boat.’ ”
Fane returned to work at the end of the summer while Shand spent the next nine months restoring a 28-foot yacht in Fiji. “Mark sold his flat in London,” Fane said. “He sold every single thing he had for this boat.” In March 1982, Mark, along with a more experienced local sailor, set out from Fiji, to Honiara, in the Solomon Islands, dropping anchor in the harbor just in time for a hurricane to hit. “The boat was like a bucking bronco,” Shand wrote. “I decided we had to get off, otherwise we were dead…. We both were cut to pieces, lacerated by the coral while being swept ashore…. The boat had no chance…. I saw her rise up once more, topple backwards, and snap in two like a matchstick. I was numb. My dream had ended. I had lost everything.”
Shand and Clio Goldsmith, at home in London, 1998; they were married from 1990 to 2009.
By Derry Moore/Camera Press/Redux.
texts.10:
Shortly after he returned to London, Shand was introduced to war photographer Don McCullin, who asked Mark to accompany him on an expedition to the Mentawai Islands, in Indonesia, to photograph the lost Sakkudei people. After 18 years covering wars from Vietnam to El Salvador for the London _Sunday Times,_ McCullin had been pushed out by the new Murdoch regime, and, as he wrote in his 1992 autobiography, _Unreasonable Behaviour,_ he wanted to “get rid of the rubbish in my mind and record the disappearing tribes of the world, before it’s too late.” McCullin, the son of a fishmonger, told me, “When I first met Mark, I didn’t think he’d be my cup of tea. He was brought up in that kind of aristocratic world. But he chose a freer world.”
In 1985, Shand and McCullin, joined by Fane, made their expedition to New Guinea (then called Irian Jaya). “One day, we found ourselves in this strange place called Otsjanep, which has a reputation for cannibalism,” recalls the photographer. “We were chased by what I thought were pirates, but they were Indonesian paramilitaries, and they surrounded us. They were pointing M16s at us. This guy who was looking after us was somebody Mark had found in Jakarta’s bus station—he did all the interpretation. The paramilitaries said, ‘You’ve been looking for skulls,’ and we said, ‘No we haven’t.’ But Mark and Harry _had_ bought some human skulls and had them in biscuit tins on the boat. The guy that Mark picked up at the bus station started saying about Harry, ‘This man friend of the Queen.’ And then he pointed to Mark: ‘This man friend of prime minister of England.’ In fact, Mark’s uncle was Sir Geoffrey Howe, the foreign secretary. He had nothing to say about me. I had no pedigree at all. But he saved our asses.”
texts.11:
Around that time, Mark began a romance with Marie Helvin, the sultry British _Vogue_ cover girl whose marriage to photographer David Bailey was near an end. In her 2007 book, _The Autobiography,_ Helvin described their first encounter, at a London dinner party: “I still remember … the sheer heat I felt when he said hello…. It didn’t take long for that initial ember of attraction to explode into a bonfire of lust.” Nonetheless, she says she turned him down when he proposed marriage, in late 1987.
That June, however, Mark had met his future wife, Clio Goldsmith, at a ball given by her uncle Jimmy Goldsmith at Cliveden, the former Astor stately home in Buckinghamshire. Clio, a daughter of Jimmy’s older brother, Teddy Goldsmith, had been previously married to Pirelli-tire heir Carlo Puri Negri. “For dinner it was a very serious older crowd, all these English politicians and aristocrats,” says Clio. “Exactly at midnight, these double doors opened and in stepped Mark and Imran Khan with a whole bunch of young, groovy people behind them. Mark and I looked at each other and that was it. We sat and we talked till six o’clock in the morning.”
Mark and Clio seemed custom-made for each other. Her father was an ecologist, polemicist, and philosopher, who traveled extensively among the tribal peoples of Africa and Asia. Clio recalled he would dictate to his secretary in full Masai gear from Kenya. Her mother was an English beauty aptly named Jill Pretty. As a young girl, Clio devoured the exotic adventure novels of the 19th-century English writer H. Rider Haggard, and Sir Richard Burton was her idol. She left home when she was 16, modeled in Paris for a few years, then in 1980 made her first film, in Rome. “It was called _La Cicala,_ the Gypsy girl,” she said. “That was me. I always played Gypsy girls or prostitutes.” When she met Mark, she had been “living in a car in Guatemala, being a textile dealer.”
texts.12:
“A few months after I met Mark, he got up one morning and he said to me, ‘I’ve got this fabulous idea. I’m going to travel India on an elephant.’ I said, ‘Wow, can I come too?’ ‘No, you can’t, because it’s a man’s expedition.’ ”
Shand published his first book, _Skulduggery,_ about his New Guinea trip, in 1987. Four years later he produced the unexpectedly affecting _Travels on My Elephant,_ which recounts his 600-mile journey on a she-elephant named Tara from the Bay of Bengal to the world’s oldest elephant market, on the Ganges River. It became an enormous best-seller and won him the British Travel Writer of the Year Award. Shand’s third book, _Queen of the Elephants,_ about the first female mahout (elephant driver), Parbati Barua, won the 1996 Thomas Cook Travel Book Award in Britain and the Prix Littéraire 30 Millions d’Amis in France, and was accompanied by a BBC documentary. Clio recalls, “We went off together on that one…. Mark and I had eight years of complete bliss. After that it got complicated.”
They had married three years after they met, in 1990, at the Laines. Clio wore a cream lace dress by Ossie Clark, and the wedding cake was in the shape of the Taj Mahal. They took a four-month honeymoon, Clio says. “Marie-Hélène de Rothschild lent us her house in Marrakech. Then we went down the Nile and to Singapore and Bali, to Mark’s house, where my father joined us.”
texts.13:
Ayesha Shand was born in 1994. As far as Mark was concerned she was named after Ayesha of Jaipur, but, for Clio, the name came from Haggard’s 1887 novel, _She: A History of Adventure,_ in which Ayesha is the 2,000-year-old white queen ruling over a tribe of central-African savages. “We bought a house at the bottom of a valley in Wiltshire,” Clio told me. “Very dark, very miserable, very isolated. Mark set off traveling, and I was alone with this baby. I had had a terrible birth, so I had to be operated on. And I was very traumatized.”
The success of his books had given Shand the legitimacy, the sense of purpose, that he’d always lacked. “He was looking for something,” says William Astor. “And it wasn’t until he met an elephant that he found it, and redeemed himself.” The books and the TV documentaries with Goldie Hawn and Julia Roberts that followed also made Shand a celebrity, complete with groupies. Astor says that the in-joke around London was that “for a whole generation of English upper-class girls, their gap year was going to India, going to the elephant camp, meeting Mark, sleeping with Mark. It was like a rite of passage.”
“One day I decided I’ve got to react,” Clio recalled. “He’d been months away, so I wrote him a note that said, ‘Gone to live in Rome with Ayesha. If you want to join us, here’s the plane ticket.’ ” For the next seven years, Mark made a halfhearted attempt to cohabit with his wife and daughter in Italy. “He was so terrible! He wouldn’t utter a word of Italian. But I loved him. In a big, big way. We decided we should go back to England and make a fresh start. Unfortunately, by that time I’d lost him, basically. And I couldn’t live with Mark in that indifferent way. It was too painful. He got very very obsessed by his charity, Elephant Family. Which was fantastic for him, and I truly recognized how wonderful it was. But our marriage just broke to pieces.” Shand and Goldsmith divorced in 2009.
texts.14:
Shand had launched Elephant Family in 2002, with Ayesha of Jaipur and London banker Sir Evelyn de Rothschild as its leading patrons. In the afterword of the 2012 edition of _Travels on My Elephant,_ Shand explained the organization’s mission:
Ninety percent of the Asian elephant population had been wiped out in the previous hundred years. Ninety-five percent of their forest homes had been destroyed to make way for plantations, farms, mines, roads, railways and villages…. The last remaining elephants were forced into tiny pockets of forest where they were competing with their human neighbours for food, water and space…. In India alone, a person kills an elephant and an elephant kills a person every single day of the year…. Elephant Family is dedicated to ending this daily battle.
Elephant Family didn’t really get going until 2004, when Shand found the 26-year-old Ruth Powys, daughter of an evangelical preacher from the north of England, who would turn out to be his perfect creative, administrative, and romantic partner. “They became this incredible force together,” says Ruth’s twin sister, Mary Powys, who joined the charity in 2008. “They were on and off for many years, but what was consistent was the huge respect and love between them. Because together they were making stuff happen.” When I asked Ruth about her relationship with Shand, she said, “Basically, I comforted him through his horrible divorce.”
The first big fund-raiser Shand and Powys pulled together was the 2006 Elephant Durbar at the Petersham Nurseries, outside London, which was attended by Prince Charles and Camilla, who had wed the previous year. Then came the Elephant Parade in London in 2010, Jungle City in Edinburgh in 2011, and the first Fabergé Big Egg Hunt, in London in 2012. Henry Wyndham, a chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, estimates the Sotheby’s auctions that were part of these events took in as much as $10 million.
texts.15:
In July 2013, the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall hosted Elephant Family’s Animal Ball, with drinks at Clarence House followed by dinner next door at Lancaster House. That November, Mark met up with his sister and brother-in-law on their official tour of India, taking them to see some of Elephant Family’s projects. “My stepfather adored him,” says Tom Parker Bowles. “They were very similar in their views. They just got on. And when they went to India, Mummy said, ‘Thank God for Mark. I’ve never been happier to see my little brother in my whole life.’ ”
“Mark was absolutely full of his new role being sort of the palace wit,” his art historian friend John Richardson says. “And Charles finally had a buddy. Mark put everybody at their ease. And he had all these stories to tell. And he told them brilliantly.”
Mark could also be relentless and rude. He wanted _more_ artists, _more_ press, _more_ real-estate tycoons to place his eggs around their buildings and sponsor them for $10,000 each. “His view was ‘You’re so fucking rich, give me the fucking money,’ ” says Ben Elliot, whose international concierge company, Quintessentially, helped organize the project. “But to get shit done, you have to be relentless.” Even the devoted Annabel admits, “He was a user and abuser; we all knew that in the family. But we all went back for more. And that’s the interesting thing.”
“When Mark died, his diary was full,” notes Mary Powys. “There were at least eight cities that had expressed interest in hosting Big Egg Hunts, including Hong Kong.” Shand’s Indian friend Uma Dubash, the sister of the last Maharaja of Morvi, told me, “There’s still a lot of work to be done for the Asian elephant, but the ground has been broken by Mark. He became the Elephant Man for a lot of Indians.”

**Mark Roland Shand** (28 June 1951 – 23 April 2014) was an English travel writer and conservationist.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3) He was the brother of Queen Camilla. Shand wrote four travel books, and as a BBC conservationist appeared in documentaries related to his journeys, most of which centred on the survival of elephants. His book _Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992. He was the chairman of Elephant Family, a wildlife foundation, which he co-founded in 2002.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-4)

## Family, education and marriage
[edit]
Mark Roland Shand was born on 28 June 1951, the third child and only son of Major Bruce Shand (1917–2006) and his wife, Rosalind Cubitt (1921–1994), daughter of the 3rd Baron Ashcombe and Sonia Rosemary Keppel, daughter of Alice Keppel. He was the brother of Queen Camilla (formerly Camilla Parker-Bowles) and Annabel Elliot.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Mark_Shand_is_the_Elephant_man-3)
Shand was educated first at [St Ronan's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Ronan's_School "St Ronan's School") in Kent[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-5) and then Milton Abbey School in Dorset. He was expelled from Milton Abbey for smoking cannabis,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-6) in response his father sent him to Australia to make a living on his own, where he had numerous jobs including working as a jackaroo on a station and a guard at an opal mine.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7) He later returned to London and worked as a porter at [Sotheby's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotheby's "Sotheby's"). Subsequently, he and his friend Harry Fane, the son of the 15th Earl of Westmorland, started a business of selling Cartier jewellery for a while.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8) He dated Caroline Kennedy, daughter of U.S. presidentJohn F. Kennedy and First LadyJacqueline Kennedy Onassis, in the mid-1970s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-9)

## Family, education and marriage
In 1990, Shand married Clio Goldsmith, a French former actress, daughter of Edward Goldsmith and niece of Sir James Goldsmith,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-10) who were all members of the prominent Goldsmith family. They lived in Rome and had a daughter, Ayesha (born 1st October 1994).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-11) Shand confirmed in 2010 that the couple were divorced.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-12) He was a godfather to one of the sons of Jemima Goldsmith, his former wife's cousin.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-13)
Shand published his first travel book _Skulduggery_ in 1987, based on an expedition to Irian Jaya in Indonesia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-14) He later became the author of _Travels on My Elephant_ (1992),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-15)_Queen of the Elephants_ (1996)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-16) and _River Dog: A Journey Down the Brahmaputra_ (2003).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-17)_Travels on My Elephant_ became a bestseller and won the Travel Writer of the Year Award at the British Book Awards in 1992.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-roland-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-mark-8)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-Shand-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shand#cite_note-19)

Mark Roland Shand was born on June 28, 1951, to Major Bruce Shand and the Honorable Rosalind Maud Cubitt. His father’s family had made its money importing calico fabric from India. Major Shand, a Sandhurst graduate, served as an officer in the 12th Royal Lancers during World War II. He spent two years in a German prisoner-of-war camp and was twice awarded the Military Cross for bravery. “Mark’s father was one of the guys on whom _The Great Escape_ was based,” says writer Gita Mehta, referring to the 1963 movie starring Steve McQueen. Don McCullin recalls, “Major Shand was the archetypal English gentleman with decorations, good manners, impeccable dress. That was quite a hallmark for Mark to live up to.” Mark’s mother was the daughter of Roland Cubitt, the third Lord Ashcombe, whose great-grandfather had made a fortune building much of Belgravia and Pimlico in the first half of the 19th century. _Her_ mother, Sonia Keppel, was a daughter of Alice Keppel—the official mistress of King Edward VII.

Bruce Shand and Rosalind Cubitt made a highly attractive couple when they married, in 1946, at St. Paul’s, Knightsbridge, with a reception following at Claridge’s. Camilla was born the following year, and Annabel two years after that. They lived in the village of Plumpton, about 50 miles south of London. Their house, the Laines, was surrounded by Rosalind’s garden, which had been laid out by the distinguished landscape designer Russell Page. Bruce Shand spent weeknights at the family’s residence in London, where he was a partner in the Mayfair wine merchants Block, Grey and Block. His passions were polo and fox-hunting, and from 1956 to 1975 he was Master of Southdown Foxhounds.
“We had this enchanted childhood,” says Annabel Elliot. “Unlike a lot of our generation, we had this incredibly warm, easy relationship with our parents. We didn’t have nannies. All our friends growing up would immediately be drawn to my mother. She was completely straightforward, and one of the warmest, kindest people.”
“Life at the Laines was wonderful,” agrees interior decorator Jane Churchill, whose parents were best friends with the Shands. “The odd thing for that sort of family is they were brought up in a completely unsnobbish way. That’s where Camilla has the edge. It’s no different to her to talk to a duke or a dustman. And Mark was the same.” Another old family friend, antique dealer Duncan McLaren, remembers, “Mark was always the joker in the pack, the one who was getting up to trouble. His mother _adored_ him. His sisters _adored_ him.”
Annabel told me that a few years before their mother died, in 1994, “Camilla and I were having lunch with her. And she said, ‘Darlings, I’ve always been completely fair between the three of you, haven’t I?’ Camilla’s and my jaws dropped. Because that was _not_ the way it was. Literally, Mark could do no wrong. There’s the theme that should run through your whole story: Mark, having been worshipped by my mother, was spoiled by women his whole life.”

Along with William Waldorf Astor III, Mark was sent to work on a sheep farm in Australia for six months. “We were each given about £100 and a plane ticket,” says William Astor.
As luck would have it, on their stopover in Delhi, the 17-year-olds ran into the grandson of Lord Mountbatten, the last viceroy of India, and spent the next several weeks touring the subcontinent in deluxe style, going from lunch at the Indian presidential palace to the Taj Mahal under army protection. In Jaipur, the boys were received by the Maharani Ayesha and her son, Prince Jagat, both of whom would become Shand’s close friends. After putting in their time in the Australian outback, “riding horses and getting thousands of sheep ready to be sheared,” Astor recalls, they spent four months meandering through Nepal, Afghanistan, and Turkey in a jeep.
Lee Radziwill got to know Mark Shand in the late 1960s at Helmsley, the shooting estate in Yorkshire that her husband Prince Stanislas Radziwill leased with Harry Ashcombe, the younger brother of Mark’s mother. “I was always so happy when I knew Mark was coming,” she says. “It was so dreary when he didn’t.”
For a long time Shand assumed that he would inherit a substantial fortune from his thrice-married yet childless Uncle Harry (known as Mad Harry). The fourth Baron Ashcombe was chairman of Holland, Hannen & Cubitts, which controlled the family’s vast property holdings in London. Unfortunately, as William Astor puts it, “he was the nicest man—and the worst businessman. He owned Pimlico and he sold it for nothing.” (According to _The Telegraph,_ the Pimlico estate, covering 27 acres, including 480 houses, was sold for £4.4 million in 1970.)

By then they were spending every February with Prince Jagat at his ancient fort in the center of Jaipur, hunting for gems by day and carousing by night. July and August were reserved for Bali, where they built, in Shand’s description, “a beautiful Robinson Crusoe house on a surfers’ beach. We lived a bohemian life, chilled-out and very anti-social.” Fane recalled, “We did some amazing trips. We did this huge sail through Indonesia in a dug-out tree.” But, Fane added, “Mark came to me one day and said, ‘Look, I really want to give up work. I want to spend my life out here, not back in the other world. Let’s sell everything and buy a boat.’ ”
Fane returned to work at the end of the summer while Shand spent the next nine months restoring a 28-foot yacht in Fiji. “Mark sold his flat in London,” Fane said. “He sold every single thing he had for this boat.” In March 1982, Mark, along with a more experienced local sailor, set out from Fiji, to Honiara, in the Solomon Islands, dropping anchor in the harbor just in time for a hurricane to hit. “The boat was like a bucking bronco,” Shand wrote. “I decided we had to get off, otherwise we were dead…. We both were cut to pieces, lacerated by the coral while being swept ashore…. The boat had no chance…. I saw her rise up once more, topple backwards, and snap in two like a matchstick. I was numb. My dream had ended. I had lost everything.”

Shortly after he returned to London, Shand was introduced to war photographer Don McCullin, who asked Mark to accompany him on an expedition to the Mentawai Islands, in Indonesia, to photograph the lost Sakkudei people. After 18 years covering wars from Vietnam to El Salvador for the London _Sunday Times,_ McCullin had been pushed out by the new Murdoch regime, and, as he wrote in his 1992 autobiography, _Unreasonable Behaviour,_ he wanted to “get rid of the rubbish in my mind and record the disappearing tribes of the world, before it’s too late.” McCullin, the son of a fishmonger, told me, “When I first met Mark, I didn’t think he’d be my cup of tea. In 1985, Shand and McCullin, joined by Fane, made their expedition to New Guinea (then called Irian Jaya). “One day, we found ourselves in this strange place called Otsjanep, which has a reputation for cannibalism,” recalls the photographer. “We were chased by what I thought were pirates, but they were Indonesian paramilitaries, and they surrounded us. The paramilitaries said, ‘You’ve been looking for skulls,’ and we said, ‘No we haven’t.’ But Mark and Harry _had_ bought some human skulls and had them in biscuit tins on the boat. The guy that Mark picked up at the bus station started saying about Harry, ‘This man friend of the Queen.’ And then he pointed to Mark: ‘This man friend of prime minister of England.’ In fact, Mark’s uncle was Sir Geoffrey Howe, the foreign secretary. Around that time, Mark began a romance with Marie Helvin, the sultry British _Vogue_ cover girl whose marriage to photographer David Bailey was near an end. In her 2007 book, _The Autobiography,_ Helvin described their first encounter, at a London dinner party: “I still remember … the sheer heat I felt when he said hello…. It didn’t take long for that initial ember of attraction to explode into a bonfire of lust.” Nonetheless, she says she turned him down when he proposed marriage, in late 1987.
That June, however, Mark had met his future wife, Clio Goldsmith, at a ball given by her uncle Jimmy Goldsmith at Cliveden, the former Astor stately home in Buckinghamshire. Clio, a daughter of Jimmy’s older brother, Teddy Goldsmith, had been previously married to Pirelli-tire heir Carlo Puri Negri. “For dinner it was a very serious older crowd, all these English politicians and aristocrats,” says Clio. “Exactly at midnight, these double doors opened and in stepped Mark and Imran Khan with a whole bunch of young, groovy people behind them. Mark and Clio seemed custom-made for each other. Her father was an ecologist, polemicist, and philosopher, who traveled extensively among the tribal peoples of Africa and Asia. Clio recalled he would dictate to his secretary in full Masai gear from Kenya. Her mother was an English beauty aptly named Jill Pretty. As a young girl, Clio devoured the exotic adventure novels of the 19th-century English writer H. Rider Haggard, and Sir Richard Burton was her idol. She left home when she was 16, modeled in Paris for a few years, then in 1980 made her first film, in Rome. “It was called _La Cicala,_ the Gypsy girl,” she said. “That was me. I always played Gypsy girls or prostitutes.” When she met Mark, she had been “living in a car in Guatemala, being a textile dealer.”

“A few months after I met Mark, he got up one morning and he said to me, ‘I’ve got this fabulous idea. I’m going to travel India on an elephant.’ I said, ‘Wow, can I come too?’ ‘No, you can’t, because it’s a man’s expedition.’ ”

They had married three years after they met, in 1990, at the Laines. Clio wore a cream lace dress by Ossie Clark, and the wedding cake was in the shape of the Taj Mahal. They took a four-month honeymoon, Clio says. “Marie-Hélène de Rothschild lent us her house in Marrakech. Then we went down the Nile and to Singapore and Bali, to Mark’s house, where my father joined us.”

Ayesha Shand was born in 1994. As far as Mark was concerned she was named after Ayesha of Jaipur, but, for Clio, the name came from Haggard’s 1887 novel, _She: A History of Adventure,_ in which Ayesha is the 2,000-year-old white queen ruling over a tribe of central-African savages. “We bought a house at the bottom of a valley in Wiltshire,” Clio told me. “Very dark, very miserable, very isolated. Ninety percent of the Asian elephant population had been wiped out in the previous hundred years. Ninety-five percent of their forest homes had been destroyed to make way for plantations, farms, mines, roads, railways and villages…. The last remaining elephants were forced into tiny pockets of forest where they were competing with their human neighbours for food, water and space…. In India alone, a person kills an elephant and an elephant kills a person every single day of the year…. Elephant Family is dedicated to ending this daily battle.
Elephant Family didn’t really get going until 2004, when Shand found the 26-year-old Ruth Powys, daughter of an evangelical preacher from the north of England, who would turn out to be his perfect creative, administrative, and romantic partner. “They became this incredible force together,” says Ruth’s twin sister, Mary Powys, who joined the charity in 2008. “They were on and off for many years, but what was consistent was the huge respect and love between them. The first big fund-raiser Shand and Powys pulled together was the 2006 Elephant Durbar at the Petersham Nurseries, outside London, which was attended by Prince Charles and Camilla, who had wed the previous year.
